narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 63.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year ranking also worked against you, though with less force. Your undergraduate GPA was the only one of these three that pulled in the opposite direction, slightly increasing the chance you might pass, but it was not enough to overcome the other signals.

In simple terms, the model saw that you finished both your first and third years near the very bottom of your class—far below the average performance of students who were admitted. Even though your undergraduate GPA of 2.4 was somewhat lower than the 3.23 average of accepted students, this was the one piece of information that gave the model a modest reason for optimism. Your LSAT score of 27, also well below the accepted average of 37, added further concern but carried less weight than your class rankings.

Your family income, gender, race, and plan to attend full-time played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT. Stronger grades and a significantly higher test score in a future application could change the outcome. Consider academic support programs or a post-baccalaureate course before reapplying.
